summary.value:
This paper addresses a challenging problem of glass surface detection and proposes an interesting bi-modal solution using RGB and NIR image pairs. The four reviewers gave split ratings, with one marginally above the acceptance bar, two marginally below the acceptance bar, and one reject. All reviewers raised valid concerns, most of which were addressed by the authors during the rebuttal. A key shortcoming, however, is that the paper focuses heavily on the experimental setup, dataset construction, and empirical results, while insufficiently analyzing the underlying physical principles that justify the use of NIR (Reviewer ysrH). Based on the current evidences, AC recommends Reject. 

AC strongly encourages the authors to enhance the analysis section to better highlight the physical grounding of the proposed method. In particular, comparisons with alternative setups—such as RGB paired with flash RGB (to isolate the effect of active illumination) and RGB paired with SWIR (to isolate the effect of spectral differences)—would substantially strengthen the paper and clarify the advantages of the chosen RGB–NIR configuration.

reviewer_concerns.value:
Reviewer P9xm (Reject) raised concerns included missing comparisons with foundation segmentation models (e.g., SAM2), narrow dataset distribution, questionable stability of Retinex decomposition, lack of out-of-distribution evaluation, and unclear broader applicability. The authors added SAM related comparisons, clarified dataset scale and diversity, justified Retinex via latent-space CTDN with ablations and latency analysis, and provided OOD examples and application discussion. Therefore, most technical concerns were addressed, though doubts about dataset breadth and framing may remain.

Reviewer NYLP (Marginally above acceptance) is overall positive, yet raised concerns focused on limited dataset diversity analysis, lack of general RGB–NIR baselines, and potential instability of Retinex preprocessing. The authors expanded dataset descriptions, added broader baselines, and showed that Retinex contributes limited overhead and improves performance via ablation. Therefore, this reviewer’s concerns are mostly resolved.

Reviewer 7XQx (Marginally below acceptance) questioned whether the method is essentially low-light enhancement plus glass detection, requested stronger visual evidence of RGB–NIR complementarity, and noted presentation and dataset issues. The authors clarified the role of enhancement, added explanations and planned visualizations of intermediate features, and addressed dataset and GT issues. So, presentation concerns are improved, but core conceptual doubts remain partially unresolved.

Reviewer ysrH (Marginally below acceptance) raised concerns included the necessity of NIR, lack of consideration of other modalities, limitations and privacy implications of NIR sensing, and limited architectural novelty. The authors mainly reframed contributions around task-specific cross-modal reasoning, yet could not provide in-depth and insightful feedbacks.

reviewer_scores.value: It is very likely that Reviewer P9xm would raise the score to Marginally below (or above) the acceptance threshold. Reviewer NYLP and Reviewer 7XQx would likely keep their scores unchanged. Reviewer ysrH, however, has the possibility of lowering the score, as this reviewer raised more fundamental questions about the paper, particularly regarding why NIR information is necessary and what physical principles justify its use. The authors did not sufficiently discuss meaningful alternatives that could demonstrate deeper understanding, for example, that SWIR might be equally effective (though with higher sensor cost), or that an RGB image with flash illumination could also be effective. While NIR benefits from both active illumination and spectral differences, making it likely more robust, these trade-offs and alternatives were not clearly articulated in the response.

comment.value:
We would like to thank you for the insightful comments for our work. Below, we address the concerns raised in the feedback.

**Reply to R1(P9xm)Q1**(The image distribution is too narrow):

  Our dataset consists of 6,192 RGB and NIR image pairs captured from nigh-time real-world scenes, and covers 12 types of daily life scenes, such as campus, hotel, and shopping mall. Compared the RGB-NIR dataset (Yan et al., 2024), our hybrid imaging system employing an active NIR light source to reconstrct the first night-time RGB-NIR dataset. In general, our dataset is a large multimodal dataset and contains varying glass/image ratios, posing a significant challenge to detect glass surface in night-time scenes.

**Reply to R1(P9xm)Q2**(Instability of the retinex decompositon, intrinsic decomposition):

  In the Retinex Decmposition stage of our method, our mehtod decomposes the input RGB and NIR images into Reflectance components and Illumination components. The SOTA unsupervised content-transfer decomposition network (CTDN) (Jiang et al., 2024) that performs decomposition in the latent space, is adopted  to obtain content-rich reflectance maps and content-free illumination maps. Just as suggested in Jiang et al., 2024, our metod first employ an encoder, which consists of cascaded residual blocks where each block downsamples the input by a scale of 2 using a max-pooling layer, to transform the input images into latent space. Initial reflectance and illumination maps are estimated from the features. Then, CTDN decompose the features into content-rich reflectance map and content-free illumination map. 

  Specifically, a cross-attention (CA) module is used to leverage the illumination map to reinforce the content information in the reflectance map. A self-attention module (SA) is adopted to further extract content information in the illumination map, which is then substracted from the illumination map and added to the reinforced reflectance map. Notably, in our mehtod, we upsample the final reflectance map and illumination map to the original resolution to ensure high detection accuracy in subsequent stages. We also fine-tune the CTDN as well as its encoder on our proposed nighttime GSD dataset.

  Existing methods typically perform decomposition in the image space to obtain the above components, which results in the content information not being fully decomposed into the reflectance map and partially retained in the illumination map. In contrast, CTDN performing decomposition within the latent space, facilitates the generation of reflectance maps containing abundant content-related details and illumination maps that remain unaffected by content-related influences, avoiding leakages. 

  In our previous experiments, we observed that since transparent glass surfaces are easily penetrated by visible and near-infrared light and lack intrinsic features, intrinsic decomposition (as the following reference[1]) struggled to yield correct albedo and norm map for glass surfaces, resulting in the loss of crucial features required for reliable glass surface detection. Therefore, for glass surface detection, instead of employing intrinsic decomposition, we adopted Retinex decomposition to process the visible and near-infrared image pairs.

**Reply to R1(P9xm)Q3**(No comparisons with segementation models like SAM2):

  SAM2 is a prompt-based general segmentation model and does not operate under the same fully automatic setting as our GSD task. It cannot leverage NIR cues and performs poorly on transparent surfaces. For completeness, we evaluated SAM2 with point prompt. We select 15 points from the ground-truth mask randomly. The results are shown in the table below. It underperforms significantly compared with our method. The ACC metric shows the proportion of the glass area that is correctly labeled, so SAM2 can accurately locate the glass area with the help of prompts. However, it is prone to over-detection, resulting in a lower IoU. Moreover, we test the SAM3 in our dataset with the text prompt 'glass'. SAM3 can segment glass regions in some scenes, but it fails in many others, leading to lower overall performance metrics. We will add these results in the revision.

**Table 1: Result of SAM2 and SAM3 in our dataset with point prompt**
*****
| Method | IoU↑  |$ F_\beta$↑| MAE ↓  | BER↓   | ACC↑   |
| -------- | :-----:| :--------: |:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
| SAM2(zero-shot) | 71.58 | 0.821  | 0.138 | 0.146 | 0.873  |
| SAM2(fine-tuning) | 78.00 | 0.845 | 0.095 | 0.094 | 0.955 |
| SAM3(zero-shot) | 60.08| 0.695  | 0.143 | 0.200 | 0.639  |
| ours | 87.98 | 0.934  | 0.047 | 0.055 | 0.936 |
*****

[1]Maralan, Sepideh Sarajian, Chris Careaga, and Yagiz Aksoy. "Computational flash photography through intrinsics." In Proc.CVPR, pp. 16654-16662. 2023.

We thank the reviewer for the careful reading of our manuscript and the constructive suggestions. Our responses to the key concerns are summarized as follows:

**Reply to R3(7XQx)Q1**(The proposed method combines low-light enhancement and glass surface detection. Visualizing enhanced inputs is recommended):

  All enhanced images are generated by the SOTA low-light image enhancement method LightenDiffusion (Jiang et al., 2024), ensuring their high quality. Table 2 in our manuscript is intended to demonstrate that even with enhanced images, existing methods cannot effectively benefit from them due to the substantial feature distribution shift between nighttime and daytime images. Our method solely adopts the unsupervised Content-Transfer Decomposition Network (CTDN) (Jiang et al., 2024) to perform Retinex decomposition on the input RGB-NIR image pair. Then, our method uses two separate encoders to extract semantics-aware, material-aware, and contextual features from the reflectance components of the two modalities. This further shows that our work is not merely a simple combination of low-light image enhancement and glass surface detection. Since our network does not rely solely on the enhanced images, we do not include them in our manuscript. Nevertheless, we provide visualizations of the reflectance components produced by the Retinex decomposition in Figures 16 and 20. Following this reviewer's suggestion, we will show the low-light enhancement results in our manuscript/supplemental.

**Reply to  R3(7XQx)Q2**(Appropriate visual features are needed to validate the effectiveness of the proposed module):

  We appreciate the reviewer's suggestion and will revise the description of the pipeline and the presentation of feature maps accordingly. Besides, Figure 5 mainly demonstrates that NIR features $X^0_n$, under the guidance of RGB features($X^0_r$ and $X^3_r$), enhance the response in glass regions. $X^i_d$ serves as an intermediate result to capture the differences between NIR and RGB features, and we visualized the resulting $M_d$. Unlike daytime images, due to the combination of nighttime conditions and active NIR illumination, noticeable differences are not confined to the glass regions, so $M_d$ does not clearly highlight the glass areas. In contrast, the attention map generated by $QK^T$ in the self-attention (SA) module clearly highlights the glass regions, which also validates the rationality of our module design. According to the good suggestion, we will shown more intermediate features in our revised supplemental file. 

**Reply to R3(7XQx)Q3**(Training and testing datasets have different glass area ratio distributions):

   Although the dataset was randomly split, the glass-area ratio distributions of the training and testing sets are not expected to be perfectly identical. In particular, we intentionally controlled the number of low glass-area images during dataset construction to avoid an overabundance of "almost no glass" samples.

**Reply to R3(7XQx)Q4**(the GDD and GSD datasets):

   GDD and GSD are benchmark datasets for single-image glass surface detection and do not include NIR (near-infrared) images. We use the same RGB image as input for both branches, and the experimental results are shown in Table 7. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance across nearly all quantitative metrics (except for F$_\beta$↑ on GSD), demonstrating our model's high suitability and effectiveness for glass surface detection.

**Reply to R3(7XQx)Q5**(Incorrect ground truth in Figure 12):

   There is a mesh screen in front of the glass in this image, which creates some ambiguity in the glass region and leads to annotation errors. We will consider replacing the incorrect ground truth in future versions.

**Reply to R3(7XQx)Q6**(A detailed analysis of failed cases is needed):

   In Appendix A.10, we originally reported the failure cases in a descriptive manner. The reason our model fails in these two cases is mainly that, when RGB (visible) information is absent, the near-infrared images provide insufficient cues to support accurate glass detection. The NIR images are presented as gray-scale and lack certain color and texture information. For example, this issue occurs in the lower-right region of the first scene and the bottom area of the second scene.

We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and constructive suggestions. Our concise responses are as follows:

**Reply to R2(NYLP)Q1**(Lacks analysis of dataset diversity):

  The metrics presented in our dataset are widely used in previous glass surface detection works. We will enhance the dataset diversity description in the revised manuscript.

**Reply to R2(NYLP)Q2**(Compares mostly with glass-specific models, broader cross-modal or RGB-NIR baselines are needed):

  Our current comparisons focus on glass-specific methods because they represent the most relevant and directly comparable approaches for the GSD task. Our model is evaluated against 17 comparison methods, including 8 glass-detection approaches and 9 state-of-the-art methods from other domains. The most relevant baseline is NRGlassNet[1], a relatively simple daytime RGB-NIR glass detection model. We have also adopted SAM 3 as an additional baseline, and the experimental results are reported in R1(P9xm)Q3. 


**Reply to R2(NYLP)Q3**(Retinex adds extra cost and may be unstable in noisy night scenes):

  In our framework, retinex decomposition is performed by the SOTA unsupervised content-transfer decomposition network (CTDN) (Jiang et al., 2024), which employs retinex decomposition in the latent space to get the content-rich reflectance map and content-free illumination map. Specifically, an encoder is first employed to transform the input images into latent space, from which the initial reflectance and illumination maps are estimated. Then, a cross-attention (CA) module is used to leverage the illumination map to reinforce the content information in the reflectance map. A self-attention module (SA) is adopted to further extract content information in the illumination map, which is then substracted from the illumination map and added to the reinforced reflectance map. We fine-tuned CTDN on our dataset, particularly for nighttime RGB-NIR data, while freezing its parameters during training our network to ensure stable and deterministic inputs. 

  This design prevents instability under noisy nighttime conditions and ensures that the decomposition acts as a lightweight, fixed operation rather than an additional trainable component that might accumulate errors. As shown in Table 4 ("w/o Retinex Dec"), removing CTDN leads to a performance drop of 0.95 in IoU, indicating that the reflectance/illumination cues provide meaningful benefits.

  We also note that CTDN contributes only a small portion of the total latency (10 ms out of 109 ms per frame on an RTX 4090). Thus, it is not the computational bottleneck of the pipeline.


[1] "NRGlassNet: Glass surface detection from visible and near-infrared image pairs." KnowledgeBased Systems, 2024.

**Reply to R1(P9xm)Q4**(Are there out-of-distribution results to show the model’s real-world generalization):

  The scenes and results shown in Figure 15,16,17,18 are not included in our dataset. We captured these images using the equipment shown in the Figure 19. We have also tested the generalizable capacity of our model in other datasets (Table 3 and Table 7). Notably, our experiments did not involve generated datasets and all the images were collected from the real world, so the model has good generalization ability in the real world images.


**Reply to R1(P9xm)Q5**(Are there more applications that can employ this method?):

  Our cross-modal fusion strategy is not limited to glass surface detection. The proposed modules can be applied to other tasks using NIR illumination, such as semantic segmentation, pedestrian/object detection and and robotic navigation in nightime and/or severe adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain and dense fog. We will add this discussion to the revised manuscript.

summary.value: This paper tackles the challenge of nighttime glass surface detection (GSD) by leveraging the complementary sensing of RGB and active Near-Infrared (NIR) imaging. The authors build the first large-scale nighttime RGB–NIR dataset with 6,192 paired images and high-quality annotations. They propose a Retinex-based dual-branch network with two key modules: RNGE, which uses RGB semantic features to enhance NIR material and boundary cues, and RNFL, which fuses RGB–NIR features via illumination-aware cross-modal attention. The method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on nighttime scenes

strengths.value:
- The work focuses on the “nighttime” domain, an underexplored yet highly practical setting ,where RGB-only cues fail under low or complex artificial illumination. The use of active NIR sensing as a complementary modality is both well-motivated and technically novel.

- The paper presents the first large-scale RGB–NIR glass surface dataset for nighttime scenes. It includes realistic environments and detailed annotations, offering a valuable benchmark for future research.

weaknesses.value:
- This paper lacks a comprehensive analysis of the diversity of the dataset, such as curved or irregular glass surfaces, extreme lighting variations, or outdoor conditions. 

- The study primarily compares against glass-specific models. It would be more convincing to include general cross-modal or RGB–NIR segmentation/detection baselines. 

- Retinex pre-processing introduces computational overhead and potential instability under noisy nighttime conditions. It would be valuable to explore lighter or integrated alternatives, such as explicitly modeling reflectance/illumination branches within the backbone itself, to reduce latency.

comment.value:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for detailed feedback and for highlighting important aspects of our work. Below, we provide further elaboration to address your concerns:

**Reply to R4(ysrH)Q1**(The necessity of using additional modality):

  Glass surface detection is a challenging task due to the lack of inherent visual characteristics and is easily concealed in the surrounding environment. Therefore, the state-of-the-art RGB image-based glass surface detection methods are not robust enough and always struggle with challenging scenes. The motivation for employing NIR images is not that the task is entirely unsolvable using RGB alone. Instead, NIR provides complementary physical cues that help address several challenging cases where RGB image-based methods consistently struggle, which means that our proposed RGB-NIR based method can be more effective, robust, and reliable. It can be seen in Table 1 that multi-modal methods generally perform better than RGB-based methods.

**Reply to R4(ysrH)Q2**(The possibility of using another modality):

  We choose NIR mainly for three reasons. First, NIR sensors are inexpensive and are widely integrated into existing RGB-NIR camera modules (e.g., surveillance cameras), making NIR a practical choice for real-world deployment. Second, NIR images provide high spatial resolution and image quality compared with thermal images or depth maps, and therefore supply clearer structural and material information for target scenes. Third, its ability to suppress reflections makes NIR particularly suitable for glass detection. Therefore, although other modalities are theoretically possible, NIR offers the best balance between physical relevance and practicality for glass surface detection. This is why we primarily focus on RGB-NIR in this work.

**Reply to R4(ysrH)Q3**(NIR camera also has many limitations):

   Since NIR shares the same imaging mechanism as RGB and has stronger penetration capability, distance does not pose a limitation for its use in everyday scenarios. Our dataset was collected in public environments, so there is no risk of privacy leakage. Moreover, during data acquisition, we intentionally avoided capturing pedestrians, as their movement could cause misalignment between paired images.

**Reply to R4(ysrH)Q4**( Novelties of the approach's framework and the contribution need to be rephrased):

  We agree that designing a novel architecture for multi-modal fusion is challenging, as many existing works adopt similar encoder-decoder structures. However, the core contribution of our work does not lie in proposing a new high-level architecture, but rather in introducing new task-specific cues and proposing cross-modal reasoning mechanisms tailored for nighttime glass surface detection, an interesting and challenging research problem that has not been addressed in the prior literatures.

The main contributions of the proposed modules can be summarized as follows:

**RNGE**: It extracts and enhances multi-scale NIR reflectance features conditioned on the RGB reflectance features by exploting the differences between the two modalities and enhancing crucial cues through self-attention. We use RGB reflectance features to enhance NIR reflectance features, rather than the reverse, as RGB images may not provide sufficient information under challenging conditions, such as extremely low-light conditions. 

**IDE**: It leverages the illumination component obtained from retinex decomposition, enabling our network to adjust the contribution of RGB and NIR features within the RNFL module.

**RNFL**: It integrates the extracted multi-modal features with the guidance of illumination differences between the two modalities estimated from the IDE module,  through a multiscale, progressive cross-modal interaction and adaptive fusion design to predict the glass surface masks.

summary.value: This submission introduces a method for glass detection at night by proposing an approach for nighttime glass surface detection.

strengths.value:
1. The author claims that this is the first method for the related topics. 
2. This work also contributes a dataset.

weaknesses.value:
1. I remain unconvinced by the rationale for employing NIR images. Is the underlying reason that the task is entirely unsolvable using the RGB modality alone? If this is the case, the authors should conduct and present more comprehensive experiments to clearly illustrate the shortcomings of existing RGB-based methods.

2. If the additional modality is necessary, why can the authors only consider NIR? Is it possible to use another modality?

3. Though the NIR camera can provide some helpful information at night, it also has obvious limitations. For example, the distance of the NIR may limit its usage. Besides, NIR light can sometimes lead to a see-through effect, which may violate privacy. 

4. For such a fusion task, it is challenging to develop a framework with novelty. From an architectural perspective, the proposed approach shares a very similar framework to previous approaches. It presents only some standard feature fusion modules. It is better to rephrase the contribution at this point.

summary.value: This paper proposed a night-time glass surfaces detection method. The reflectance and illumination components of RGB and NIR images are first decomposed, respectively. Then the semantics-aware features from the RGB reflectance are extracted to enhance the material-aware features from the NIR reflectance. The multi-modal features of the lighting and material information are fused together to detect glass areas. The authors also constructed a night-time glass surface detection dataset containing 6,192 RGB-NIR image pairs with the corresponding manually annotated glass surface masks. Comparative experimental results showed that the proposed method outperformed the existing methods.

strengths.value:
This paper introduced a relatively new problem of night-time glass surface detection, and showed the proposed method yields better performance than the compared existing methods.

A new dataset of night-time glass surface detection was constructed, which is welcomed in the research community.

weaknesses.value:
1) The proposed night-time glass surface detection problem is basically a combined problem of low-light image enhancement and glass surface detection. Specifically, the proposed Retinex decomposition module decomposes input low-light image into reflectance and illumination components, which is similar to the behavior of low-light image enhancement. Table 2 seems to provide the related experimental results, however it is not easy to figure out the benefit of the proposed method in this experimental setting, since the performance of low-light enhancement was not guaranteed. It is recommended to visualize the input low-light enhanced images as well.
 
2) The architectures and their explanations in Sec. 4 are easy to follow, and therefore the related equations such as (1), (2),(3) are not required. Furthermore, instead of naïve explanation about the procedures of architecture, more evidences and discussions are recommended to be provided to support that the proposed architecture exploits complementary features between RGB and NIR effectively. In this context, proper visualization of the complementary features between RGB and NIR images are also recommended. 

Also, the explained behavior of the proposed architecture in Figure 4 can be confirmed by visualizing intermediate features such as X^i_d and X^i_f. 
M_d in Figure 5 does not properly highlight the glass area. 
It is also recommended to discuss the results of intermediate feature maps in Figure 5.

questions.value:
My main concerns are given in the Weaknesses section.

In addition, some minor questions are as follows:

- Why are the distributions of the glass area ratio different between training dataset and testing dataset, even though the two datasets are randomly split? 

- Are the existing datasets of GDD and GSD in Table 7 also multimodal datasets including NIR images? 

- The GT in the 3rd row in Figure 12 seems to fail to capture the opened window, while NRGlass successfully captured.

- In A. 10, instead of naïve reporting the failure cases, discussion why the proposed method fails on the images is recommended.
